doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: Union rules about quitting a band
summary: Discussion of giving two weeks' notice and Marty paying his own fare from Toronto.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: A quick question about the union. It seemed like they had a fairly together system about, you just don’t walk out on a band, with the business of having to give two weeks. Let’s suppose you walked out on a band. What was the — what could happen to you?
But would you lose your union card?
I don’t know it’s never happened to me. And I don’t know anybody that it’s ever happened to. But I mean if you were working, like say for instance you’re traveling on the road with a band?

Well I guess that’s a matter of a personal thing between the leader and whoever is walking out on the band. Maybe the band leader would say good riddance, I wanted to get rid of him anyway so the guy quit, good riddance. Or he might say “oh you can’t do that to me,” like Teddy Powell said, “no you gave a two week notice which means you’ve got to go 14 days.” And the 13th day was a day off, I had to go to Toronto. And I was making like $130 a week or something, and I had to pay my own carfare back from Toronto, which was ten, twenty dollars, but it hurt me in the pocket, see? And I said why couldn’t he say I’ll get a piano player in New York? He was in New York. He could have made a phone call to his agent or somebody who was booking the band and say get me a piano player in New York and have them meet us up in Toronto. Simple. There were so many guys in those days, my God everybody was there.
Well he was probably in a bad mood because Charlie was leaving at the same time, and he said I’ll take it out on you.
